reading.rtitle: The Comma That Decided Who Was Covered
paras: Two drafts of the same clause left the same office three days apart. Draft A read: the contributors who delivered their work before 1 March shall be paid the full fee. Draft B read: the contributors, who delivered their work before 1 March, shall be paid the full fee. The words are identical. Nobody in the firm flagged the difference, and the difference is eleven fees, because nineteen people contributed and only eight of them delivered before the first of March.

In Draft A the clause carries no commas, so it narrows the group: the fee goes to the contributors who were on time, and to nobody else. In Draft B the same words sit between two commas, and a clause between commas narrows nothing at all. It names the whole group and then adds a fact about every member of it, which means Draft B promises the fee to all nineteen and, into the bargain, states something that is not true, since eleven of them delivered in April. The scope of the two clauses is different, and so is the money.

This is not an unusual accident, and it is not a sign of careless drafting. The clauses that end up in front of a court are almost never the badly written ones; they are the ones where two competent people read the same correct sentence in two different ways and neither of them was being unreasonable. The remedy is not more words. A longer clause offers more places for a second reading to hide, and most of the extra length is boilerplate that nobody has read since it was first copied. The safest version of this clause is also the shortest one: the full fee shall be paid only to those contributors who delivered on or before 1 March. It is watertight, and there is nothing left in it for a comma to decide.

listenings.text: When somebody in their first year asks me a question about punctuation, I stop them, because in a clause the comma is not punctuation. It decides who is inside the group and who is outside it, and I have seen that difference measured in millions. So here is the test I give them, and it takes four seconds. Cover the clause with your hand and read what is left. If the sentence still means what you wanted it to mean, the clause is only adding a fact and it takes commas. If the sentence suddenly goes too wide, if it now covers people you never intended to cover, then the clause is doing work, and it must not have commas around it. That is the whole of it. Now, the thing I want you to take away is not the test. It is this. The drafts that end up in front of a judge are almost never the badly written ones. Bad drafting gets caught. What gets litigated is the clause where two competent people read the same correct sentence in two different ways, and neither of them was being unreasonable, and both of them are certain.

Everybody believes that a longer contract is a safer contract, and it is the most expensive false belief in this profession. Length does not protect you. Length adds places for a second reading to hide, and most of the extra length is boilerplate that nobody has read since the day it was first copied from somewhere else. We rewrote a standard agreement for a client two years ago, in plain English, keeping every obligation exactly as it was. It came out at less than half the length. What happened next is the part I use in every talk I give. The arguments about what it meant stopped almost completely, and the clients started reading it, which nobody in the room had predicted and one or two people did not entirely welcome. And to any student who is nervous about writing simply, because it does not sound like a lawyer: simple and vague are opposite things. The fear is not really about precision. It is about sounding like somebody who belongs. A watertight clause is usually a short one, and the short one is much harder to write.
